description:
Our team is working on The Earth Information Jukebox, transforming NASA Earth science data into interactive soundscapes to make climate and environmental information more accessible and engaging.

We're looking for teammates with skills in frontend development, UI/UX design, data visualization, audio programming, and Earth science. Beginners willing to learn and contribute are welcome.
summary: GeoOrchestra is an interactive web application that turns NASA rainfall measurements and Earth science imagery into sound. Developed for The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, it allows users to explore 295 months of Philippine precipitation data, from June 2000 to December 2024, through synchronized maps, graphs, tables, and generated audio. Musical Sonification translates rainfall into notes, while Geophony conveys changes through synthesized rain textures. Users can also listen to spatial patterns in NASA precipitation imagery through a frame sweep. The project aims to make Earth science more accessible to students, educators, and blind or low-vision users, while allowing them to inspect the values behind what they hear. Because of this, sound becomes another way to explore the data and discuss its meaning.
details:
GeoOrchestra connects rainfall data, visual displays, and generated sound through one playback clock. Its Numerical workspace uses NASA GPM IMERG Final Monthly V07B precipitation estimates at a 0.1° resolution. Users can explore the Philippines, Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao, or individual grid cells, with the selected date carried across the table, map, graph, and piano roll.

The sound communicates both rainfall amount and its context. Higher rainfall produces higher notes, while a background hum represents the same calendar month’s average over 2001–2022. For instance, a teacher could play several Julys and let students hear whether each month was wetter or drier than that reference before inspecting the graph. Geophony offers another interpretation through rain density and texture. These sounds are designed representations of satellite estimates, rather than environmental recordings.

The Visual feed uses NASA’s IMERG Daily Precipitation Climatology imagery. A west-to-east sweep translates latitude into pitch and image-derived rainfall intensity into loudness. Users can explore cells, select a region, and read descriptions of the displayed patterns. However, the seasonal numerical linkage is reconstructed from monthly measurements and labelled approximate; values decoded from image colours are also distinguished from the original measurements.

The application was developed using TypeScript, React, Tone.js, Zustand, Zod, and Vite, with Python, NumPy, Pillow, and Shapely for data preparation. Prepared files allow playback without a live NASA connection. Its creative contribution is the combination of inspectable musical mappings, environmental textures, and spatial listening within one application.

The team considered scientific traceability, listening complexity, performance, and accessibility. Presets and spoken briefings introduce the sounds, while keyboard controls, captions, screen-reader announcements, and Unicode braille charts provide other ways to explore the information. Missing values remain separate from zero rainfall. Braille hardware compatibility and some listening and timing checks still need verification, so the intended accessibility benefits should be evaluated with users.
dataRefs: GPM IMERG Final Monthly Precipitation V07
NASA SVS 5478: IMERG Daily Precipitation Climatology, 2001–2022
